outcome: The question remains open. By the Euclid-Euler theorem it is equivalent to whether there are infinitely many Mersenne primes; no proof or disproof has appeared since 26 January 2024. A 52nd Mersenne prime (2^136279841-1) was found by GIMPS in October 2024 using GPU hardware, which is a new example but does not bear on the infinitude question per se. Two self-published preprints (Frank Vega, first posted April 2024; Ikorong Anouk Gilbert Nkodo/Nemron, posted September 2025) claim routes to resolving the question, but neither has been peer-reviewed, digested by experts, or gained any traction in the mathematical community, so neither meets the bar for `claimed` or higher. No AI system was found to be involved in any of this activity in a role beyond incidental mention.
summary: This bullet asks whether there are infinitely many perfect numbers, which (via the Euclid-Euler theorem) is equivalent to the still-open question of whether there are infinitely many Mersenne primes. Nothing in the window (26 Jan 2024 - present) settles or narrows this question in the sense required by §3.1: the only concrete development is the discovery of the 52nd Mersenne prime, 2^136279841-1, by GIMPS in October 2024 (the first GIMPS discovery found using an Nvidia GPU rather than Prime95/CPU, via a cloud VM volunteered by Luke Durant) — per §3.1 this is explicitly excluded ('a new example... does not narrow where an answer could hide'). I also examined two self-published preprint claims flagged by triage. (1) Frank Vega's 'Note for the Perfect Numbers' (first posted to EasyChair/ResearchGate/Cambridge Open Engage/ScienceOpen starting 22 April 2024, i.e. inside the window, with revisions through July 2024) claims to prove there are only finitely many Mersenne primes via an elementary argument on the sigma function. It has never been peer-reviewed or accepted by any journal, and search turned up no expert engagement, citation, or refutation discussion of it at all — it sits alongside a long history of Vega preprints on P vs NP, the Riemann hypothesis, and related famous problems that have not been accepted by the field (one exception, a Robin's-criterion paper, was accepted by the Ramanujan Journal, but that is a different problem). Given no expert has engaged with or endorsed the argument, and note that at least one version needed a self-acknowledged fix to a flawed upper-bound step, it does not meet the `claimed` bar for a serious contested claim so much as an un-digested fringe assertion; I record it as not changing the status. (2) Ikorong Anouk Gilbert Nkodo's 'A Curious Note around the Perfect Numbers Problem' (Zenodo, 27 August/6 September 2025) merely proposes a conjecture whose truth would imply a proof by contradiction — it does not itself claim a proof, and the author has a long history of similar self-published notes on twin primes, Goldbach, and other famous conjectures with no evidence of mathematical-community acceptance. I also checked whether any AI lab or system (DeepMind AlphaProof/AlphaEvolve, GIMPS software, etc.) has been involved: DeepMind's 'formal-conjectures' GitHub repository tracks 'infinitude of Mersenne primes' as issue #134, but this is purely a formalization bookkeeping task (writing the open conjecture's statement in Lean/Mathlib for a benchmark corpus), not any attempt to prove it, and involves no AI-generated mathematics. A 2025 paper called 'The emergence of the Mersenne Star...bridging physics and artificial general intelligence' (Arab Journal of Basic and Applied Sciences, 2025; also on Zenodo/PhilArchive) describes geometric patterns among the finitely many known Mersenne primes and speculates about future AGI applications to prime-finding, but makes no claim about infinitude and involves no AI system producing any part of its content — it is patent-application-adjacent numerology dressed in AI branding, not a mathematical result in scope. GIMPS itself uses GPU compute (Prime95/Mlucas/Prime-Gpuowl) for primality testing, which is exhaustive/certified computation, not an AI system, consistent with §6.2's exclusion of computer-assisted search from AI-role coding. In sum: the problem is squarely open, nothing in the window changes that, and no genuine AI involvement was found anywhere near it.
competing_reading: One could argue Vega's preprint, despite lacking peer review, should be coded `claimed` on the grounds that it is a serious, structured resolution attempt by an author with at least one accepted paper in a reputable journal (Ramanujan Journal, on a different problem). I did not adopt this reading because (a) no expert digestion, citation, or engagement with this specific paper was found in any venue searched, (b) the author's oeuvre includes many parallel unaccepted claims on other famous problems (P vs NP, etc.), which is exactly the pattern §6.1 warns is 'not enough' for `claimed` even from a prestigious-seeming author, and (c) at least one version needed a self-described fix to a flawed bounding step, suggesting the argument was not robust even to its own author's later scrutiny.
what_would_settle_it: Either an accepted journal publication or a Terence-Tao-tier expert blog digestion working through Vega's or Ikorong's argument line by line and either endorsing or refuting it; alternatively, any future genuine proof or disproof of the Lenstra-Pomerance-Wagstaff conjecture (which predicts infinitely many Mersenne primes) from a source that gets picked up by the number theory community.
